title: CHEM1A Practice Quiz — Objective 9: Bonding II → Materials — MO, IMFs, Solids, Solutions (DRAFT pending Gilley approval)

items.stem: A diatomic molecule's MO diagram holds 6 electrons in bonding orbitals and 2 in antibonding orbitals. Its bond order is:
items.explain: Bond order = (bonding − antibonding)/2 = (6 − 2)/2 = 2. Adding instead of subtracting gives 4; forgetting to halve gives 4 as well; counting only bonding gives 3 — the formula has all three moves.

items.stem: Which bond order predicts the STRONGEST, SHORTEST bond between two atoms?
choices: They are all equal once the molecule forms
items.explain: Higher bond order = more net bonding electrons = stronger and shorter. Bond order 0 predicts no molecule at all.

items.stem: Nitric oxide, NO, is a HETERONUCLEAR diatomic — two different atoms — but the bond-order machine runs the same way. Its molecular-orbital configuration is (σ2s)²(σ*2s)²(π2p)⁴(σ2p)²(π*2p)¹. Its bond order is:
items.explain: Count the plain and the starred, subtract, halve: bonding 2 + 4 + 2 = 8, antibonding 2 + 1 = 3, bond order (8 − 3)/2 = 2.5 — fractional orders are legal, and the lone unpaired π* electron also makes NO paramagnetic. 3 forgets the antibonding π* electron; 2 double-counts it; 5.5 adds instead of subtracting.

items.stem: Which molecule can hydrogen-bond with its own kind?
items.explain: Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to N, O, or F. NH₃ qualifies. PH₃ and H₂S have H on P and S — close, but not on the list; CH₄'s H sits on carbon.

items.stem: Which substance has ONLY dispersion forces between its molecules?
items.explain: Dispersion is the only force nonpolar molecules get. HBr and SO₂ add dipole-dipole; NH₃ adds hydrogen bonding. Every option HAS dispersion — the question is who has nothing else.

items.stem: Which hydrogen halide has the HIGHEST boiling point?
choices: They increase steadily with size, so HBr wins by mass
items.explain: HF hydrogen-bonds (H on F) and that beats the dispersion advantage of the heavier halides. Option D is the pure-size reasoning that misses the hydrogen-bond anomaly.

items.stem: At room temperature F₂ and Cl₂ are gases, Br₂ is a liquid, and I₂ is a solid. What force grows down the group to cause this?
choices: Dispersion — it strengthens as electron count and size grow
Dipole-dipole — the heavier halogens are more polar
Covalent bond strength within each molecule
items.explain: All four are nonpolar: dispersion is the only intermolecular force present, and it scales with polarizability. The bonds INSIDE the molecules are not what melting and boiling break.

items.stem: Steam at 100 °C burns far worse than liquid water at 100 °C because the steam:
choices: Releases its heat of vaporization as it condenses on skin
items.explain: Same temperature — the difference is ΔHvap (2256 J/g) dumped during condensation. Phase changes move heat without moving temperature.

items.stem: How much heat is required to melt 50.0 g of ice already at 0 °C? (ΔHfus = 334 J/g)
choices: 0 kJ — melting needs no heat once at 0 °C
items.explain: Flat segment: q = m × ΔHfus = 50.0 × 334 = 16 700 J = 16.7 kJ. Option B uses q = mcΔT machinery where none applies; option C mistakes constant temperature for zero heat.

items.stem: Beyond the critical point, a substance:
choices: Becomes a supercritical fluid — the liquid/gas distinction disappears
items.explain: Past critical T and P there is no boundary left between liquid and gas — one fluid phase. No pressure can liquefy a gas above its critical temperature.

items.stem: Dry ice sublimes (solid → gas, no liquid) at ordinary pressure because 1 atm is:
choices: Below CO₂'s triple-point pressure — the liquid region is out of reach
Too cold for liquids to form
items.explain: CO₂'s triple point sits at 5.11 atm. Below that pressure the warming path crosses straight from solid to gas — the liquid region only exists above it.

items.stem: Diamond melts above 3500 °C and conducts no electricity. It is best classified as:
items.explain: One giant lattice of covalent bonds — melting means breaking real covalent bonds, hence the extreme temperature; every electron is pinned in a bond, hence no conduction.

items.stem: A solid does not conduct electricity — but it conducts well when melted or dissolved in water. It is:
choices: Ionic — the ions are locked in the lattice until freed
items.explain: Ionic solids have charge carriers (the ions) that cannot move until melting or dissolving frees them. Metals conduct as solids; molecular solids have no charge carriers at all.

items.stem: How many atoms does one SIMPLE cubic unit cell own?
items.explain: Eight corner atoms × one-eighth each = 1. Counting the corners as whole atoms gives the classic wrong answer of 8.

items.stem: How many atoms does one BODY-centered cubic unit cell own?
choices: 2 — eight corners at one-eighth, plus the body atom
items.explain: 8(⅛) + 1 = 2. Nine counts corners whole; 4 is the face-centered census.

items.stem: Iodine (I₂, nonpolar) dissolves best in:
items.explain: Like dissolves like, said in forces: I₂'s dispersion-only toolkit matches hexane's. Water's hydrogen-bond network won't open up for a solute that offers nothing back.

items.stem: A gas dissolves MOST in a liquid when the conditions are:
choices: Temperature and pressure do not affect gas solubility
items.explain: Gas solubility rises as temperature falls and as pressure rises (Henry's law) — why cold sealed soda stays fizzy and warm open soda goes flat.

items.stem: 2.0 mol of solute dissolved in 4.0 kg of water has a molality of:
choices: It cannot be computed without the solution volume
items.explain: m = mol solute ÷ kg SOLVENT = 2.0 ÷ 4.0 = 0.50 m. Option D is molarity thinking — molality never needs a volume.

items.stem: Which concentration unit does NOT change when the solution's temperature changes?
choices: Molality — it is built from masses only
items.explain: Molarity's denominator (liters) expands and contracts with temperature; molality's (kilograms of solvent) cannot. That is why colligative equations use molality.

items.stem: Which 0.10 m aqueous solution has the LOWEST freezing point?
choices: 0.10 m K₃PO₄ — four particles per formula unit
items.explain: Colligative properties count particles: i = 4 beats 3, 2, and 1 at equal molality. Ignoring dissociation makes all four look identical — the i-blind error.

items.stem: A 0.500 m aqueous solution of a NONELECTROLYTE boils at: (Kb = 0.512 °C/m)
items.explain: ΔTb = i·Kb·m = 1 × 0.512 × 0.500 = 0.256 °C, ADDED to 100.00. Subtracting gives 99.74 (boiling goes up, freezing goes down); 100.51 forgets the 0.500; 102.56 invents i = 10.

items.stem: To find a molar mass from freezing-point depression, the correct order of steps is:
choices: ΔTf → molality → moles of solute → grams ÷ moles
items.explain: The measured ΔTf gives m (divide by i·Kf); m times kilograms of solvent gives moles; the weighed sample mass over those moles is the molar mass. Molarity never appears.

items.stem: 3.0 g of a nonelectrolyte in 100.0 g of water freezes at −0.93 °C (Kf = 1.86 °C/m). Its molar mass is:
items.explain: m = 0.93/1.86 = 0.50 m; moles = 0.50 × 0.1000 kg = 0.050 mol; MM = 3.0/0.050 = 60. g/mol. Halving or doubling errors come from the kilograms step.

items.stem: Which of these is a COLLOID?
items.explain: Milk's dispersed particles are colloid-sized — big enough to scatter light (Tyndall), too small to settle. Salt and sugar water are true solutions; sand settles — a suspension.

items.stem: The reliable way to tell a SUSPENSION from a colloid is that a suspension:
items.explain: Suspension particles are large enough for gravity to win. Colloids scatter light but never settle; solutions do neither.

items.stem: A COLLIGATIVE property depends on:
choices: How many dissolved particles there are
items.explain: Number, not identity — that single idea is the whole colligative toolbox, and it is why the van 't Hoff factor exists.

items.stem: Two liquids that mix in ALL proportions — like ethanol and water — are called:
items.explain: Miscible = mutually soluble without limit. Immiscible is the opposite (oil and water); saturated describes a solution at its solubility limit.
